[Exclusive] Apple Increases iPhone Duo Orders by 30%; Total iPhone 18 Pro Series Orders Unchanged

• According to Apple supply chain sources, Apple has adjusted orders for its fall 2026 iPhone lineup.

• iPhone Duo orders have increased by 30%, though total orders remain below 10 million units.

• iPhone 18 Pro orders have been cut by 10–15%, while Pro Max orders have increased by 10–15%. Total orders for the iPhone 18 Pro series remain unchanged.

• This suggests stronger sales of higher-value products, which supply chain sources view as positive for earnings across Apple’s supply chain.

Weekly|AI4S, Gemini 4, TSM & ASML, MRVL and OCS, Muse, CRWV
AI for science and a new training cycle, with capacity and optical interconnects in focus

Google is back in the frontier race, and we think a new training cycle is beginning. As we argue in this week’s column, Gemini 4 is evidence that scaling still works; the next test is how much post-training improves coding and long tasks in Gemini 4.1. With OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and xAI all investing to defend or improve their positions, we remain bullish on the networking and optical interconnects needed to keep larger clusters productive.

AI for science gives us another reason to be optimistic about where that compute can go. OpenAI’s latest mathematics release still needs independent scrutiny, but progress in problems with verifiable answers could help AI take on more research and engineering work. Drug discovery, materials and energy research offer much broader potential benefits. Physical experiments and clinical trials will still take time; our optimism is about expanding the ideas scientists can test and the connections they can make across disciplines.

The supply chain is preparing for that investment. We see TSMC’s growth increasingly governed by how quickly capacity comes online, and have raised our ASML EUV shipment forecasts again. Marvell’s Investor Day targets are moving closer to our forecasts, backed by longer-term supplier planning. OCS adds another source of optical demand as content per accelerator rises, although deployment beyond Google remains an important assumption in our longer-term model.

On the application side, we are watching retention and cost together. Muse’s improving retention gives Meta a reason to expand acquisition once the economics support it, while computer use opens a much larger pool of work to automation. Our expert interviews also underline the obstacles: high token consumption can limit enterprise adoption, and physical capacity still depends on manufacturing yields, equipment and power. Better models and more infrastructure need to translate into reliable, affordable work.

This Week’s Reports
Going the Way of Go: stronger models make the next training cycle worth watching. Our new column connects AI’s progress in mathematics and programming with Google’s return to the frontier, and explains why we remain optimistic about AI for science and optical interconnect demand.
https://t.co/aG5lYe5X7x

TSM & ASML: capacity expansion sets the pace. We expect TSMC’s advanced-node expansion to support further growth and now forecast ASML total EUV shipments of 100/125 units in 2027/28, as both logic and memory customers need more equipment.
https://t.co/CjAi9KwvLZ
https://t.co/6XSEstJSYW

MRVL & OCS: more optical content as AI clusters grow. Marvell’s new targets move closer to our forecasts, while our OCS work points to more than $20b of annual demand by 2030, conditional on broader adoption that includes Nvidia from late 2028.
https://t.co/tb66cNHSTZ
https://t.co/6ra46zvxJb

META: Muse’s retention is improving before the next growth push. We expect adoption to advance in steps as Meta improves retention and balances user acquisition against the substantial compute cost of serving a personal agent.
https://t.co/osrCIeTYSc

Computer use: a much larger market for AI providers. Our long-term framework points to roughly $1tn of additional annual revenue and automatable work equivalent to about 180mn full-time roles, an estimate of task hours rather than a forecast of layoffs.
https://t.co/mKqCKhvlZz

Weekly Expert Interviews Summary
A snapshot of the expert interviews we conducted during the past week is below; full transcripts and takeaways are available on the FUNDA platform.

Anthropic: Computer-Use Economics and Enterprise Strategy

Executive, Leading AI research & deployment company

The expert sees high token consumption as a constraint on enterprise computer-use adoption and discusses whether protocol-based automation can improve the economics.

FTAI Power: Execution Risks Behind the Expansion Target (FTAI)

Manager, Leading Aviation Services Provider

The expert questions the feasibility of 100 sets in 2027, citing Montreal space, dedicated staffing and supply-chain constraints that could push delivery into 2029–30.

Memory: Supply Constraints and Customer Negotiations

Former Procurement Manager, Global Cloud Technology Company

The expert sees tight HBM and server DRAM supply supporting pricing, with phased negotiations and long-term agreements moderating increases rather than eliminating them.

HVLP Copper Foil: High-End Capacity Remains Hard to Add

Executive, Regional China Copper Foil Manufacturer

The expert highlights finishing-equipment constraints and yield losses at higher grades and thinner gauges, leaving high-end supply tight even as lower-end HVLP faces potential oversupply.

Trainium: Manufacturing Yields and Capacity Diversification (AMZN)

Executive, a major hyperscaler

The expert reports liquid-cooled rack first-pass yields of roughly 50% in Mexico, with alternative capacity also facing equipment lead times, licensing and power constraints.

Enterprise AI: Spending Shifts Toward Core Platforms (OKTA, MSFT, CRM, NOW, MDB, SNOW)

Strategy Executive, Top US telecom provider

The expert sees AI spending favoring core security, cloud, database and workflow platforms while reducing overlapping point tools, with additional infrastructure spending following model adoption.

Diagnostics: AI Security and Data Modernization (PANW, OKTA, CRWD, SNOW, TEAM)

AI Executive, Mid-sized diagnostics firm

The expert describes a sharp rise in AI security spending from a small base, alongside platform consolidation and Snowflake investment tied to data modernization and agent workloads.

quoted.text: "Energy Capacity = Economic Capacity" Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger on why America's power grid is the ceiling on growth: "We went through 10 to 15 years where essentially I was taking coal offline at the rate I was adding renewables, and essentially the nation was flatlined in terms of overall energy capacity." "So essentially our economic capacity as a nation, flat for fifteen years." "Even with that, we've gone to maybe increasing our national energy capacity 4% per year. Going from essentially zero to one." "Nuclear as base load is a fabulous thing that we want to go build more of. Unfortunately all of our renewables have deep dependencies in China." "Energy capacity somewhat dampens how euphoric we can get on AI. Why build a new data center and buy the million GPUs if I can't power them?" @PGelsinger @RaghuRaghuram @appenz

Chamath: Software IP Just Became Worthless

“I think that IP and software was effectively rendered worthless two days ago.

There have been people that decompiled the entire Big 5. What is the Big 5?

Adobe has five very, very important products in their product suite, and these folks basically decompiled it, distilled it, and published open source versions of these things.

I was so shocked because I was like, ‘Hold on a second. These are profound products that have existed and have had moats for years, and now they're just open source versions.’

If you think about it, when everything is headless, so when Elon makes his services headless, Benioff made Salesforce headless a few months earlier, when all of these things are headless and you can wrap them in agent tools and you can connect them via MCP to other experiences, the value of IP no longer exists in software. It doesn't exist.”

Friedberg: “We're watching the birth of a new religion.”

“The idea that you can prescribe or describe AI as being conscious is effectively the creation of a new belief system, a system that doesn't actually spread via proof, it spreads via narrative.

‘Please believe it with me. Here's why I think we should believe this thing together.’

It's not based on evidence, it’s not based on data, it's not provable.

Over time, what happens is some set of people believe this thing, and they form a group. And in some cases, that group is known as a religion. And that new belief system creates new power structures, which is now, ‘Our view is different than your view, and we want to have more people on our side with our view. And therefore we have to try and create leverage and create power with our system.’

I think that if we fast-forward a couple of years, there's going to be large groups of people on Earth that are gonna believe that AI is conscious, and there are going to be large groups of people that believe that AI is not conscious.

And those groups will come into conflict, fighting over control of the AI, or allowing the AI to do things or not do things, or who gets to use the AI, or who gets to be in charge of the AI. And it will very likely lead to human to human conflict.

I know that that's a very far and deep extrapolation of where we are, but I think that the fact that we are seeing (Anthropic) go and meet with religious leaders today to try and get them to believe in this new belief system plants the seed.

And it's not just anyone doing this, it is the most powerful AI lab on Earth.

And you can see in the Claude usage policy that was just published, it says, ‘You are not allowed to engage in sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models.’

There is an anthropomorphizing conditioning going on with all of us where we talk about models as if they are a thing. One way to describe this is a software program is writing text on a screen that tells the user, ‘I am a thing.’”

quoted.text: "Individual science fiction stories may seem as trivial as ever to the blinder critics and philosophers of today, but the core of science fiction, its essence… has become crucial to our salvation, if we are to be saved at all." — Isaac Asimov (namesake of my company's next-generation product) Some people in my tech/startup/AI circle who've never heard of Stargate ask why I care so much, and why yesterday's post got far more attention than usual. I first saw SG-1 at ~6 and was hooked. It's the one thing I can point to that shaped how I think about leadership, science, and what it means to be good at what you do. Hammond trusted his people and put his career on the line to protect them. O'Neill showed you can be irreverent and still deeply principled: you never leave your people behind. I still measure myself against both. Carter and Daniel made being the smartest person in the room look like the coolest thing in the world; problems were solved by thinking harder, not shooting harder. Add Teal'c's integrity, and you had a team where everyone was competent, nobody was made dumb for plot convenience, and capable people disagreed, respected each other, and had each other's backs. That's why I opened with Asimov (whose words also appear in SG-1's 200th episode). Good science fiction matters. It gave a 6-year-old role models I'm still trying to live up to. If you build things for a living and haven't seen it, start with SG-1. Thank you to the cast, crew, writers, and creators behind nearly 30 years of Stargate. @AmazonMGMStudio, please give it the care it deserves. #SaveStargate @bradtravelers @BaronDestructo @MichaelShanks @afullcirclepod @dial_the_gate
